title: Adobe Drops 29% YTD: Should You Buy, Sell or Hold the Stock?
detail:

Adobe ADBE shares have dropped 29.1% year to date (YTD), underperforming the broader Zacks Computer and Technology sector's return of 17.5%. The weakness appears to reflect investor concerns over intensifying competition from AI-native creative platforms, uncertainty surrounding AI monetization, modest recurring revenue growth, pressure on profitability and leadership transition risks.

The company has been playing a catch-up role in the AI domain, not only against established players like Microsoft MSFT, Alphabet GOOGL and Salesforce CRM, but also from AI-native companies like OpenAI, Midjourney and Canva. YTD, Adobe shares have underperformed Alphabet's 9.3% drop, Salesforce's decline of 12.8% and Microsoft's appreciation of 9.7%. So, what should investors do with Adobe stock? Let's find out.

ADBE Stock's Price Performance
Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

Adobe Faces Multiple Challenges

The rapid proliferation of AI-powered content creation tools is challenging Adobe's traditional competitive advantages in creative software. AI-native platforms capable of generating images, videos, designs and marketing content through natural-language prompts are reducing dependence on traditional creative applications such as Photoshop, Illustrator and Premiere. Adobe is responding by embedding conversational AI and autonomous creative agents into its flagship applications. However, investors remain concerned that generative AI could commoditize certain creative workflows, increase pricing pressure and weaken ADBE's ability to sustain premium subscription pricing.

Meanwhile, AI-first ending Annualized Recurring Revenue (ARR) exceeded $650 million and surged more than 150% year over year. AI-first offerings still represent a relatively small portion of the overall recurring revenue base. Adobe expects ARR growth of 10.2% by the end of fiscal 2026, suggesting that strong adoption of new AI offerings has yet to meaningfully accelerate companywide recurring revenue growth. Investors have been skeptical about how quickly increasing usage of Firefly, AI Assistant and agentic workflows will translate into sustained revenue acceleration.

Adobe expects fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 revenues between $6.80 billion and $6.85 billion, implying approximately 1% sequential growth at the midpoint. The guidance suggests relatively modest near-term sequential revenue momentum despite rapidly growing AI engagement. Adobe also projects a non-GAAP operating margin of approximately 44% for the fiscal fourth quarter, below its fiscal 2026 target of approximately 45%. Continued investments in AI infrastructure, product development and customer acquisition could constrain margin expansion over the near term.

Salesforce, Inc. (CRM), headquartered in San Francisco, California, offers customer relationship management software that allows businesses to access, manage, and share sales information. Valued at $190 billion by market cap, the company also develops applications focused sales, customer service, marketing automation, application development, and analytics, enabling businesses to build custom workflows, and enhance operations with tools like Slack, Tableau, and MuleSoft. The cloud giant is expected to announce its fiscal third-quarter earnings for 2027 in the near term.

Ahead of the event, analysts expect Salesforce to report a profit of $2.41 per share on a diluted basis, down 9.4% from $2.66 per share in the year-ago quarter. The company has consistently surpassed Wall Street's EPS estimates in its last four quarterly reports.

How Risky Is ServiceNow Stock?

ServiceNow (NOW) stock fell 26.9% on October 29, 2026, the day after the company reported fiscal Q3 2026 adjusted earnings per share that missed analysts' estimates. News reports tied the fall to management's guidance for slower growth in contracted revenue in Q4. The S&P 500 slipped 0.4% that day, and ServiceNow now trades 41.3% below its highest close of the past year. This fall belonged to ServiceNow rather than the broader market, making past market drops only a partial guide. When the whole market has dropped before, has ServiceNow fallen further than the S&P 500, and how long did it take to come back?

ServiceNow Stock Has Usually Fallen Further Than The Market

ServiceNow stock fell an average of 20% during the 11 market shocks it has traded through since listing in 2012, compared to 13% for the S&P 500 over the same windows. Its largest drop among those periods occurred during the 2022 inflation shock, when the stock lost 46% while the index lost 24%. The 2015-2016 global growth scare hit the stock almost as hard, with a 39% decline against a 12% market drop. The 2020 COVID-19 crash was an exception. ServiceNow fell 30% during that span, slightly less than the S&P 500's 34% decline. The deepest fall since the company listed was larger than any of these events, with the stock losing 64.5% from its close on January 28, 2025, to its close on April 10, 2026.

Recovery times to the earlier high varied widely. A typical rebound took 1.2 months from the low close to the old peak, but after the 2022 fall the wait stretched to 12.9 months. The stock made it back every time. That record covers the market shocks only: at $109.67, the stock remains far below the $234.08 close where its deepest fall began.

Sales Still Grow Fast, But ServiceNow's Margins Have Shrunk

ServiceNow reported fiscal Q3 2026 revenue of $4.11 billion, up 20.5% from a year earlier. This marked the company's slowest growth over its last five quarters. Annual growth averaged 22.1% over the past three years, compared to 6.2% for the S&P 500 as a whole.

The company keeps less of each sale than it did a year ago. Reported operating margin fell to 9.4% in fiscal Q3 2026 from 16.8% in fiscal Q3 2025. Gross margin dropped to 70.5% from 77.3% over the same year. Using management's own adjusted measure, the operating margin for the quarter was 32.5%, coming in above guidance. Management expects that adjusted margin to reach 31.5% for full-year 2026, up 50 basis points from a year earlier.

Key Takeaways

Twilio shares fell 17% after a third-quarter beat and a raised 2026 outlook, as its fourth-quarter guide called for organic growth of 11%-12%, down from 16%.

The guide and an early 2027 floor of 10% organic growth suggest this year's pickup is fading.

Salesforce and RingCentral are chasing the same AI customer-engagement spending, and neither is growing faster than Twilio.

At about 38x forward earnings going into the report, Twilio's stock had little room for slower growth.

Twilio (TWLO:NYSE) beat Wall Street's estimates for the third quarter and raised its outlook for the year. Shares are down 17% today anyway.

The problem is the fourth quarter. Twilio guided to organic revenue growth of 11%-12%, down from 16%, and non-GAAP operating income of $300 million to $310 million, below the $326 million it just earned. That matters for Salesforce (CRM:NYSE) and RingCentral (RNG:NYSE) too, since they're chasing the same AI customer-engagement budgets.

The beat got smaller

Third-quarter revenue rose 20% to a record $1.56 billion, ahead of the $1.51 billion analysts expected. It was the sixth straight quarterly increase:

Twilio (TWLO): total revenues, $ billions, last 8 quarters (to September 30, 2026) (TIKR)

But on the call, analyst Elizabeth Elliott noted that Twilio beat its own guidance by more than usual in the first half, while this quarter's beat was "a little bit more modest and more normalized." Management said the smaller beat came mainly from a modest slowdown in messaging, its biggest product.

Growth is coming back to earth

Management's early look at 2027 calls for at least 10% organic growth, with $1.35 billion each of non-GAAP operating income and free cash flow. Analysts already expect growth to settle in the low teens:

Twilio (TWLO): revenue, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2023-2028 (TIKR)

That's about 12% growth in 2027, and Twilio's 10% floor gives analysts no reason to raise it.

That's a problem for a stock that traded at about 38x forward earnings at Thursday's close, and still trades around 30x after today's drop.

Salesforce's Agentforce and Data 360 annual recurring revenue reached nearly $3.9 billion in its quarter to July 31, up over 210%. Adobe (ADBE) shares have lost 55.1% since their December 6, 2024 high, and that fall is the reason to look again. Adobe's free cash flow over the last four quarters equaled 10.8% of its market value at the October 29 close, compared with 4.2% for the median S&P 500 company. Cash that plentiful for the price means a sound business on sale or one the market expects to shrink, so which is Adobe?

Adobe's Free Cash Flow Is Still Rising

Adobe generated $10.6 billion in free cash flow, the cash left after running the business and paying for equipment, during the four quarters to August 28, 2026. This was up from $9.6 billion a year earlier. Like profit, this cash belongs to shareholders whether Adobe pays it out or not. Over time, a company's share price tends to rise alongside the cash it produces for owners, especially when that figure is growing.

Subscriptions generate this cash, making up $6.56 billion of Adobe's $6.76 billion revenue in fiscal Q3 2026. Revenue rose 12.0% over the last twelve months, following a 10.7% increase the year before. Equipment took 2.0% of its cash from operations over those twelve months, showing Adobe spends little to stay in business. The company keeps a large share of each sale as profit, recording an operating margin of 35.7% against 18.5% for the S&P 500.

Adobe owed $6.76 billion on August 28, 2026, while holding $5.64 billion in cash and short-term investments. The company paid a $0.26 billion interest bill over the last twelve months, against $9.27 billion of operating profit. Looking solely at these accounts, Adobe resembles a growing business priced cheaply rather than one in decline.

Why Investors Pay So Little For Adobe's Cash

Investors may worry that Adobe's growth will fade as AI changes software. Leadership is also changing: the shares fell 6.7% on September 4, 2026, after Adobe named Anil Chakravarthy as its next CEO, starting December 1. During its September 10, 2026 call, management itself said every software-as-a-service company will go through a shift to AI agents.

Annual recurring revenue, the yearly value of Adobe's subscriptions, stood at $27.5 billion at the end of fiscal Q3 2026. This was up 11.2% from a year earlier. For the full fiscal year, management targets slower annual recurring revenue growth of 10.2%.

Management has chosen to win new users with free versions of its apps rather than raise prices. It said price increases might have brought short-term relief but would matter less than new user adoption. These free creative apps now draw more than 100 million monthly users, up more than 70% in a year.

Shares of ServiceNow (NOW) fell 26.9% on Thursday, October 29, 2026, while the S&P 500 slipped 0.3%. The decline followed the company's October 28 earnings report for the third quarter of 2026. In that quarter, subscription revenue grew 20.5% from a year earlier, excluding currency effects. So why did the shares fall so hard?

ServiceNow Missed On Earnings And Forecast Slower Backlog Growth

ServiceNow reported adjusted earnings per share of $1.00 for the quarter, falling short of the $1.02 estimate. Revenue reached $4.107 billion, just above the expected $4.095 billion. News reports linked the slide in the stock to that earnings miss, which came alongside a raised AI outlook: management lifted its year-end target for AI contracts to at least $1.7 billion. Other reports tied the fall at the open to the company's forecast for slower growth in contracted revenue.

The company's guidance pointed two ways. Management expects subscription revenue to grow 21.5% in the fourth quarter, excluding currency effects. However, it expects growth in its current backlog to slow to 18.5%, down from 21% in the third quarter. Management called this contracted revenue a good, if not perfect, guide to future revenue. The company added that strong early renewals had pulled deals out of the fourth quarter and into the third.

Did Other Software Stocks Fall With ServiceNow?

They did, but by far less. All five companies on ServiceNow's Trefis peer list fell that session. Declines ranged from 2.8% for Snowflake to 7.3% for Atlassian, and ServiceNow's drop was more than three times the largest of them. XLK, the fund that tracks ServiceNow's Information Technology sector, lost 1.2%, while the Nasdaq Composite index fell 1.4%.

News reports said software stocks fell in premarket trading on October 29 after results from Fortinet and ServiceNow, deepening worries about AI disruption in the sector. ServiceNow moved with its group, but most of its fall was its own.

Where Does ServiceNow Stock Stand Now?

ServiceNow had not fallen this much in a single session at any point in the prior 365 days. Its largest one-day fall in that span had been 17.7% on April 23, 2026. Since October 28, 2025, the stock has lost 41.5%, while the S&P 500 returned 13.3%.

The shares closed at $109.67, well below their 12-month closing high of $186.94 on October 30, 2025. They remain above the closing low of $83.00 set on April 10, 2026. Over the six months since April 30, the stock is still up 24.2%. Since September 30, it has lost 18.2%.
